identification.summary: HummingBad is an Android malware family that Check Point says it first reported in February 2016. It installs a persistent rootkit, generates fraudulent ad revenue and installs additional fraudulent apps [S1][S3]. Check Point tied it to Yingmob, a Beijing-based ad company that also runs a legitimate ad analytics business [S1][S3]. This is a criminal ad-fraud operation, not a state-sponsored APT group; the record's 'group' framing refers to the Yingmob-linked development team [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Check Point: first reported February 2016 [S3]; public attribution report published mid-2016 [S1][S2]. Lookout dates the related Shedun family to November 2015 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: Naming conflict: Lookout argued HummingBad is Shedun (also called GhostPush, AndroidOS_libskin, right_core) [S4][S5], while ElevenPaths concluded it is a distinct threat [S6]. Cheetah Mobile's 'Hummer' is reported by secondary coverage to be the same malware as HummingBad, based on shared infrastructure and the rooting file right_core.apk [S6]. These vendor cluster boundaries are not merged here. The record's existing '85 million devices' figure describes devices that installed at least one of roughly 200 Yingmob apps, not devices infected with HummingBad; about 10 million devices downloaded a malicious one [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Commercial: Check Point attributes the operation to Yingmob, a Chinese (Beijing) advertising company [S1][S3]. No government sponsorship is asserted in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Check Point presents the Yingmob link as a finding from its research; the sources do not give a formal confidence level [S1][S3].
attribution.basis: Check Point says malware samples led to Yingmob repositories, and that HummingBad shares command-and-control server addresses and enterprise-certificate use with the iOS malware YiSpecter, which it also links to Yingmob [S1][S3]. Check Point describes a 25-person 'Development Team for Overseas Platform' working on several projects [S2].

objectives: Financial: fraudulent ad revenue from fake ad clicks and fraudulent app installs. Check Point estimated more than $300,000 per month, about $3,000 per day from clicks and about $7,500 per day from fraudulent installs [S1][S2]. Check Point also warned that control of the infected devices could be sold or turned to data theft [S1][S3].

regions: China (about 1.6 million devices per Check Point)
India (about 1.35 million devices per Check Point)
targeting.notes: Check Point reports most affected devices in China and India [S2][S3]. Targeting is opportunistic and consumer-focused; no sector-specific or government targeting is stated in the sources gathered. The Check Point report raises, but does not document, a risk of data theft or sale of device access [S1][S3].

capabilities.summary: Check Point describes a staged infection: a first component attempts to gain root access with a rooting exploit, and if that fails a second component shows a fake system update notification to trick the user into granting system-level permissions [S1][S3]. Once established it keeps a persistent rootkit, clicks ads fraudulently and installs additional fraudulent apps [S1][S3]. Lookout notes that the exploits used by related rooting-adware families are not new and have been used by popular rooting tools [S5].

campaigns.name: Shedun/Shuanet/Kemoge trojanized adware reporting (related, disputed overlap)
campaigns.summary: Lookout reported the Shedun rooting-adware family in November 2015. Lookout later said HummingBad is another name for Shedun, a claim ElevenPaths disputed [S4][S5][S6].

campaigns.name: HummingBad first reported
campaigns.summary: Check Point says it first reported the HummingBad rootkit and ad-fraud malware in February 2016 [S3].

campaigns.name: Check Point attribution to Yingmob
campaigns.summary: Check Point published research tying HummingBad to Yingmob and estimating about 10 million infected devices and more than $300,000 per month in revenue, with almost 85 million devices having installed at least one of about 200 Yingmob apps [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Lookout: spike in Shedun, also known as HummingBad
campaigns.summary: Lookout published a blog post describing a rise in Shedun detections and treating HummingBad as the same family [S4]. Secondary coverage reports Cheetah Mobile counting about 1.4 million infections per day in the first half of 2016 for its 'Hummer' trojan [S6].

diamond.adversary: Yingmob, a Beijing ad company with a 25-person overseas-platform development team, per Check Point [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Android rooting exploits, fake system-update prompt, persistent rootkit, fraudulent clicks and installs [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: A control panel referencing about 200 apps, and C2 addresses shared with the iOS malware YiSpecter [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Android consumers, concentrated in China and India [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial ad-fraud motive inside a legitimate ad-tech business; no state tasking is stated [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Unpatched or rootable Android devices and users who accept fake system update prompts; app distribution through channels that host Yingmob apps [S1][S3].

gaps: I could not open the Check Point blog, the Check Point report PDF, or the news articles with WebFetch (DNS failure in this environment). Details here come from search-result summaries of those pages and need confirmation against the primary documents [S1][S2][S3].
Exact publication dates are month-level for several sources; day-level dates were not confirmed except for the Lookout post (2016-07-06) [S4].

Unresolved vendor disagreement over whether HummingBad is a distinct family (Check Point, ElevenPaths) or Shedun renamed (Lookout); relationship to Cheetah Mobile's Hummer rests on secondary coverage [S4][S6].
No public evidence gathered of state sponsorship, victim data theft, or sale of device access; Check Point's warnings are risk statements [S1][S3].
Activity after 2016, and any Yingmob response or enforcement action, were not found in the sources gathered.
The record has no MITRE ATT&CK group ID; no group mapping was verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Personal and BYOD Android phones, and unmanaged third-party app stores, are the relevant terrain; the sources show consumer targeting, not defense targeting [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor is a commercial ad-fraud operator with a development team, rooting exploits and an app-distribution pipeline; its stated aim is revenue [S1][S2]. STEP 3: The template is a trojanized app, rooting exploit, fake system-update prompt, persistent rootkit, then fraudulent ad and install traffic [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued ad fraud on consumer devices in China and India, with incidental exposure of personnel devices. MDCOA, which the sources raise only as a risk, is Yingmob or a buyer repurposing rooted devices for data theft or as a botnet [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: rooted or persistently modified Android devices, unexpected fake system update prompts, and unexplained app installs and ad traffic [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat this as a commodity mobile-malware risk to personnel devices, not a tracked state actor; monitor mobile threat defense telemetry for rooting and fake update prompts [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: mobile device management and BYOD policy, not offensive or defensive cyberspace operations, govern the response. (3) Mission assurance: keep rooted or unmanaged Android devices off sensitive networks and away from official data [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through normal CTI and mobile-security channels; the family-naming disputes mean indicators should be matched by sample hash, not family name alone [S4][S6].
